name: Digital Markets Act
evidence_rating: moderate: eight studies with causal designs since the 2026-10 broadened search (choice screens cut Google and Chrome shares slightly; Google's results-page redesign raised traffic to airlines and smaller comparison sites by 14-29%; event studies), alongside industry-funded consumer surveys and think tank reviews; headline benefits and the Commission's indicators still not measured
summary: The DMA has changed gatekeeper conduct (choice screens, steering, alternative app stores, consent, less self-preferencing on Amazon) and produced EUR 1.59bn of fines, but none of the six promised indicators is reported systematically and the EUR 13bn consumer-surplus estimate has not been assessed. Causal studies find large default effects for browsers (Firefox +91% on iOS), a one-third drop in Amazon's self-preferencing after designation, but no shift to rival map services; one small study finds lower start-up entry and investment. Theory (Madio, Manenti & Motta 2026) supports the DMA's equal-access design.

indicators.objective: Address market failures to ensure contestable and competitive digital markets for increased innovation and consumer choice
Enhance coherence and legal certainty to preserve the internal market
Enhance coherence and legal certainty / limit diverging national regulatory interventions
indicators.indicator: Number of regulatory interventions at the national level
indicators.evidence: Not reported in the 2026 review. The review records stakeholder concerns about fragmentation and parallel national enforcement and requests for guidance on Article 1(6), but gives no count.

indicators.objective: Enhance coherence and legal certainty / ensure coherent interpretation of obligations
indicators.indicator: Number of clarification requests per year
indicators.evidence: Not reported. The review describes regulatory dialogue and possible guidelines but gives no count of clarification requests.

indicators.objective: Address gatekeepers' unfair conduct / prevent self-preferencing
indicators.indicator: Number of compliance interventions by the Commission per gatekeeper per year
indicators.evidence: Activity reported, not as the indicator: non-compliance proceedings opened against Alphabet, Apple and Meta (March 2024) and Apple (June 2024); two specification decisions on Apple interoperability (March 2025); one investigation into Apple's choice obligations closed after changes. Seven gatekeepers designated. Independent evidence of conduct change: Amazon's search-rank advantage for its own products fell from about 30 to about 20 positions soon after designation (Waldfogel 2024).

indicators.objective: Address gatekeepers' unfair conduct / prevent self-preferencing
indicators.indicator: Number of sanction decisions per gatekeeper per year
indicators.evidence: Four fines in two years of application: Apple EUR 500m (anti-steering) and Meta EUR 200m (pay or consent), 23 April 2025; Alphabet EUR 460m (search self-preferencing) and EUR 430m (Google Play anti-steering), 23 July 2026. Total EUR 1.59bn. Apple's decision is under appeal.

indicators.objective: Contestable markets / prevent unfair access and data practices
indicators.indicator: Share of users multi-homing with different platforms or services
indicators.evidence: Not measured by the Commission (review says it will monitor switching). Independent evidence on one remedy: after Google removed the Maps link from EU search results, users searched for 'google maps' instead; no robust shift to rival map services (Pape & Rossi 2026).

indicators.objective: Contestable markets / prevent unfair access and data practices
indicators.indicator: Share of users switching between different platforms and services
indicators.evidence: Commission cites company figures only (Aloha +250% new users; Firefox daily users doubled on iOS in DE and FR). Independent causal estimate: Firefox usage +91% on iOS and +13% on Android vs counterfactual after the choice-screen mandate; Safari declined on iOS with gains mostly to Chrome (Akesson et al. 2026). Consent: >45% of users (up to 90%) refuse data combination under Art 5(2).

indicators.indicator: Consumer surplus +EUR 13bn per year (about +6% vs baseline)
indicators.evidence: Not assessed in the 2026 review, which says impacts are not yet fully observable.

indicators.indicator: Cross-border trade gain of EUR 92.8bn by 2025

indicators.objective: Growth and jobs (Digital Single Market-wide, not DMA-specific)
indicators.indicator: GDP +0.44-0.82% and 307-561 thousand FTEs from a more efficient Digital Single Market
indicators.evidence: Not assessed; the figure is borrowed from Digital Single Market estimates and is not attributable to the DMA alone.

indicators.indicator: Greater innovation potential among smaller businesses
indicators.evidence: Mixed. Commission review: new third-party app stores on iOS (Epic, Aptoide, AltStore PAL) and gains for alternative browsers. Yang (2025): DMA reduced start-up entry and investment in DMA-related industries (difference-in-differences, 1,034 records). Oxera (2021, Amazon-funded experiment): such rules likely reduce innovation.

literature.citation: Akesson, J., Amlani, K., Cepeda Suarez, R., Chissell, E., Hunt, S., Luca, M. & Petrie, G. (2026), Active Choice Interventions at Scale: Browser Defaults under the Digital Markets Act, NBER Working Paper 35112 (first issued April 2026 as "The Effect of Choice Screens on Mobile Browser Usage: Evidence from the EU Digital Markets Act")

literature.headline: Searches for 'google maps' +21% in EU vs non-EU; no robust gain for Bing Maps, Mappy, OpenStreetMap; total Google Maps desktop traffic unchanged; visit duration -5%, bounce rate +16%
literature.quality: strong design; one remedy only
literature.title: The DMA's Google Maps experiment

literature.citation: Madio, L., Manenti, F. M. & Motta, M. (2026), Platform Tying and its Effects, CEPR Discussion Paper 21771 (version of 21 July 2026)
literature.title: Platform Tying and its Effects
literature.method: theory (two-sided market model with simulations)
literature.headline: Tying a gatekeeper's own service can harm consumers who never use the gatekeeper, by shrinking rivals' seller base; demotion of rivals is always welfare-reducing in their simulations; a common-access rule of the DMA type removes the harm and remains profitable for the platform
literature.summary_plain: A theory paper showing why favouring a platform's own services can hurt even consumers who reach rivals directly, and that the DMA's equal-access approach removes this harm while remaining profitable for the platform. It does not measure the DMA's actual effects.
literature.quality: theory, not impact evidence; presented at "The Economics of the DMA" workshop (Brussels, 2025) and to DG Competition

literature.citation: Waldfogel, J. (2024), Amazon Self-preferencing in the Shadow of the Digital Markets Act, NBER Working Paper 32299
literature.title: Amazon Self-preferencing in the Shadow of the Digital Markets Act
literature.method: causal-leaning: before/after gatekeeper designation, compared with 142 other brands (8m+ search results, 22 Amazon domains)
literature.headline: Amazon's own products ranked about 30 positions better than comparable products; shortly after Amazon's designation as gatekeeper (Sept 2023) the advantage fell to about 20 positions, with no change for other brands; the change appeared in Europe and elsewhere
literature.summary_plain: Using over 8 million Amazon search results, the study finds Amazon's ranking advantage for its own products fell by about a third soon after the EU designated it a gatekeeper - and the change also showed up outside the EU.
literature.quality: strong data; not peer-reviewed; designation-timing comparison, no formal control market (change was global)

literature.citation: Farronato, C., Fradkin, A. & MacKay, A. (2023), Self-Preferencing at Amazon: Evidence from Search Rankings, AEA Papers and Proceedings 113: 239-243 (NBER w30894)
literature.title: Self-Preferencing at Amazon: Evidence from Search Rankings
literature.method: descriptive/econometric (pre-DMA baseline)
literature.headline: Documents that Amazon-branded products rank higher in Amazon search than observably similar products (pre-DMA baseline for the self-preferencing ban)
literature.summary_plain: Pre-DMA evidence that Amazon ranks its own-brand products higher in search results than similar products - the kind of conduct the DMA's self-preferencing ban targets.
literature.quality: context, not a DMA effect

literature.citation: Motta, M. (2023), Self-preferencing and foreclosure in digital markets: Theories of harm for abuse cases, International Journal of Industrial Organization 90: 102974
literature.title: Self-preferencing and foreclosure in digital markets: Theories of harm for abuse cases
literature.method: theory
literature.headline: Sets out when self-preferencing by platforms can foreclose rivals and harm consumers; underpins the rationale for ex ante self-preferencing rules
literature.summary_plain: Explains the economic mechanisms by which a platform favouring its own products can exclude rivals - the theory behind the DMA's self-preferencing ban.
literature.quality: theory, not impact evidence
literature.verified: cited by Madio-Manenti-Motta; listed on author homepage

literature.citation: Motta, M. & Peitz, M. (2020), Intervention triggers and underlying theories of harm: expert advice for the Impact Assessment of a New Competition Tool, report for DG Competition
literature.title: Intervention triggers and underlying theories of harm

literature.method: expert assessment (ex-ante)
literature.headline: One of the expert reports the Commission commissioned for the New Competition Tool / DMA impact assessment, on structural competition problems and theories of harm
literature.summary_plain: An expert report commissioned by the Commission that fed into the impact assessment behind the DMA, setting out when intervention in digital markets is justified.
literature.quality: ex-ante expert opinion; cited in SWD(2020) 363 part 2
literature.verified: citation seen in impact assessment (search result); report text not read

literature.title: The Magical Number 2 (Minus Two): An Empirical Analysis on the Efficacy of Choice Screens to Increase Competition in Digital Markets
literature.venue: Working paper (draft 2025-07-17), NYU School of Law; presented at KGI Digital Competition Conference 2026
literature.method: matrix completion (causal panel estimator, related to synthetic control/DiD) on monthly StatCounter country panel, EU countries vs non-EU high-income donor pool, 2017-early 2025, bootstrap CIs
literature.outcomes: Google Search mobile market share; Chrome mobile browser share
literature.headline: DMA choice screens lowered Google's EU mobile search share by about 0.56 points (95% CI -0.71 to -0.39) and Chrome's share by about 1.80 points (95% CI -2.20 to -1.41).
literature.summary_plain: After the DMA forced phones in the EU to show choice screens, Google's and Chrome's market shares fell, but only by about half a point and two points. The author concludes choice screens barely dent dominant positions.
literature.period_geography: 2017-early 2025; EU member states vs non-EU high-income countries
literature.quality: Causal panel design with explicit counterfactual; StatCounter page-view data is a noisy proxy; single-author draft, not peer reviewed.
literature.citation: Omar Vasquez Duque (2025), The Magical Number 2 (Minus Two): An Empirical Analysis on the Efficacy of Choice Screens to Increase Competition in Digital Markets, Working paper (draft 2025-07-17), NYU School of Law; presented at KGI Digital Competition Conference 2026

literature.authors: Joan Calzada, Néstor Duch-Brown, Xavier Fageda, Nicandro Quirós
literature.title: Who benefits from Google's SERP? The impact of the DMA on the Air Travel Market
literature.venue: Working paper (Universitat de Barcelona / JRC), January 2026; presented at KGI Digital Competition Conference 2026
literature.method: difference-in-differences on domain-level Similarweb traffic data, four EU countries vs UK and US controls, Nov 2023-Dec 2024
literature.outcomes: organic search, direct and referral web traffic to airline and flight comparison websites
literature.headline: Google's DMA-driven search page redesign raised organic search traffic to low-cost airlines by 14-28% on desktop and 8-22% on mobile, and to smaller flight comparison sites by up to 28.9%, with no significant change for Skyscanner or Booking.com.
literature.summary_plain: When Google removed its own Google Flights box from EU search results to comply with the DMA, more people clicked through to smaller airlines and smaller flight comparison sites. Big airlines and big comparison sites saw little change.
literature.period_geography: Nov 2023-Dec 2024; four EU countries vs UK and US
literature.quality: Credible DiD with pre-trend checks; Similarweb traffic estimates are modelled; one sector; one co-author at the Commission's JRC.
literature.interested_party: One co-author is employed by the European Commission (JRC)
literature.citation: Joan Calzada, Néstor Duch-Brown, Xavier Fageda, Nicandro Quirós (2026), Who benefits from Google's SERP? The impact of the DMA on the Air Travel Market, Working paper (Universitat de Barcelona / JRC), January 2026; presented at KGI Digital Competition Conference 2026

literature.authors: Victorine Verlooy, Monty Lukas Meier, Vincent Heimburg, Maximilian Schreieck
literature.title: The Impact of the EU's Digital Markets Act: An Event Study
literature.venue: ECIS 2025 Proceedings (European Conference on Information Systems), paper ECIS2025-1916
literature.method: event study of gatekeeper stock returns around DMA announcement and implementation events
literature.outcomes: investor reactions (abnormal stock returns of gatekeepers)
literature.headline: Gatekeeper stocks reacted positively to DMA regulatory announcements, but this optimism faded during the implementation stage (abstract gives no magnitudes).
literature.summary_plain: Investors initially reacted well to news about the DMA, perhaps expecting more competition and value, but that reaction faded once the rules had to be put into practice.
literature.period_geography: DMA announcement to implementation (approx. 2020-2024); listed gatekeeper firms
literature.quality: Standard event-study design; small number of firms and events; abstract only, magnitudes not seen.
literature.citation: Victorine Verlooy, Monty Lukas Meier, Vincent Heimburg, Maximilian Schreieck (2025), The Impact of the EU's Digital Markets Act: An Event Study, ECIS 2025 Proceedings (European Conference on Information Systems), paper ECIS2025-1916

literature.title: What About Us? Consumer Response to the Digital Markets Act
literature.method: survey of 3,500 consumers (500 each in 7 Central and Eastern European countries), Ipsos online panel, July 2025, quota sampled; descriptive statistics
literature.outcomes: consumer-reported friction, privacy concern, platform usage, DMA awareness
literature.headline: 39% of respondents report needing more steps for tasks that used to be simple, about one-third find online services less seamless since DMA changes, and 80% are unfamiliar with the DMA.
literature.summary_plain: A survey of consumers in seven Central and Eastern European countries found many people say online services became more cumbersome after DMA changes, while most still rely on Google and Meta and few know the law exists.
literature.period_geography: July 2025; Slovakia, Czechia, Hungary, Slovenia, Croatia, Latvia, Lithuania
literature.quality: Self-reported perceptions, no counterfactual; attribution to the DMA rests on respondents; authors recommend repealing the DMA.
literature.interested_party: Survey commissioned by EPPP; ECIPE states support from industry partners; authors advocate repeal or reform of the DMA
literature.citation: Matthias Bauer, Dyuti Pandya (ECIPE) (2025), What About Us? Consumer Response to the Digital Markets Act, ECIPE Occasional Paper, October 2025

literature.title: Impact of the Digital Markets Act (DMA) on consumers across the European Union: Results from a survey with 5,000 consumers
literature.method: online survey of 5,000 consumers in 20 EU member states, 28 April-15 May 2025; descriptive statistics
literature.outcomes: consumer-reported search time, service quality, personalisation, willingness to pay for pre-DMA services
literature.headline: Two-thirds of respondents say they now have to search longer than before the DMA; 35% report worse map services and 42% of frequent travellers say flight and hotel results are less helpful.
literature.summary_plain: An industry-commissioned survey of 5,000 Europeans found most say finding things online got slower and less convenient after the DMA, and many would like the old services back.
literature.quality: Recall-based perceptions without counterfactual; question framing attributes changes to the DMA; commissioned by an industry body.
literature.interested_party: Commissioned by CCIA Europe (trade association whose members include gatekeepers)
literature.citation: Nextrade Group (for CCIA Europe) (2025), Impact of the Digital Markets Act (DMA) on consumers across the European Union: Results from a survey with 5,000 consumers, Nextrade Group report, September 2025

literature.title: What Happens to App Prices when Developers Pay Lower Commission Fees? Evidence from the European Union
literature.venue: Analysis Group study, November 2025 (hosted by Apple)
literature.method: before-after comparison of prices 90 days before and after enrolment in Apple's DMA alternative business terms, ~21,000 apps/in-app purchases, 41m+ transactions; no control group
literature.outcomes: App Store prices; pass-through of commission cuts; distribution of savings
literature.headline: Despite commission rates falling about 10 percentage points, developers kept prices the same or raised them on 91% of products; more than 86% of the EUR 20.1m in savings went to non-EU developers.
literature.summary_plain: When Apple cut its fees for EU apps under the DMA, app makers mostly did not lower prices for users; they kept the savings, and most of the money went to developers outside the EU.
literature.period_geography: March-September 2024 enrolment cohorts; EU App Store storefronts
literature.quality: Descriptive before-after design without control group; Apple data; does not cover alternative marketplaces.
literature.interested_party: Funded by Apple, a designated gatekeeper
literature.citation: Jane Choi (Analysis Group) (2025), What Happens to App Prices when Developers Pay Lower Commission Fees? Evidence from the European Union, Analysis Group study, November 2025 (hosted by Apple)

literature.title: The Commission's Seven Claims, Tested
literature.method: structured qualitative assessment of the seven core claims in the Commission's April 2026 DMA review, against published evidence
literature.outcomes: contestability, consumer welfare, user data control, legal certainty
literature.headline: Argues the Commission's evidence of DMA success (e.g. 250% more Aloha browser users, Firefox iOS users doubling in Germany and France) is vendor-reported input counts without a counterfactual, and that net consumer-welfare effects are mixed and for several provisions likely negative.
literature.summary_plain: A critical think-tank scorecard of the Commission's own DMA review: it says the Commission counts activity (new app stores, more browser downloads) rather than real benefits to users and ignores costs.
literature.quality: Structured critique, no new data; relies on selected secondary studies; strongly critical prior position.
literature.interested_party: ICLE is a long-standing DMA critic and receives funding from technology companies
literature.citation: Dirk Auer (ICLE) (2026), The Commission's Seven Claims, Tested, International Center for Law & Economics

literature.title: DMA implementation sinks 30% of clicks and bookings on Google Hotel Ads
literature.method: comparison of Google Hotel Ads click volumes for 3,450 hotels in DMA vs non-DMA markets, 1 Jan-22 Apr 2024 (difference-style comparison, no formal model)
literature.outcomes: Google Hotel Ads clicks and direct hotel bookings
literature.headline: Google Hotel Ads clicks fell about 30% in DMA-affected markets relative to non-DMA markets in the three months after Google's DMA changes.
literature.summary_plain: A hotel booking-technology firm found that after Google changed EU search results for the DMA, hotels got about 30% fewer clicks from Google's hotel ads compared with markets outside the EU.
literature.period_geography: Jan-Apr 2024; EU vs non-EU markets, 3,450 client hotels
literature.quality: Simple treated-vs-control comparison on a vendor's client base; short window; no statistical testing reported.
literature.interested_party: Mirai sells hotel direct-booking and metasearch services
literature.citation: Javier Delgado (Mirai) (2024), DMA implementation sinks 30% of clicks and bookings on Google Hotel Ads, Mirai blog, May 2024

literature.title: DMA impact on hotels: 0.8% loss of direct reservations
literature.method: before-after comparison (8 months either side of 19 Jan 2024) of Google Analytics 4 booking attribution for 3,000+ hotels, EU vs non-EU
literature.outcomes: share of direct hotel bookings by source (Google Hotels, Ads, organic, metasearch)
literature.headline: Google Hotels' share of EU hotels' direct bookings fell from 13.4% to 8.9%; after partial recapture via other channels, the net loss of direct reservations was about 0.8%.
literature.summary_plain: Using booking data from over 3,000 hotels, the firm found the DMA changes cut bookings coming via Google's hotel box, but hotels won most of this back through other Google channels, for a net loss of under 1% of direct bookings.
literature.quality: Descriptive share comparison on vendor client base; attribution-model dependent; no statistical inference.
literature.interested_party: Mirai sells hotel direct-booking and metasearch services
literature.citation: Pablo Delgado (Mirai) (2024), DMA impact on hotels: 0.8% loss of direct reservations, Mirai blog, October 2024

literature.title: First bloom: increased consumer choice after eighteen months of the DMA
literature.method: structured qualitative assessment of compliance changes and open non-compliance issues (submission to the Commission's DMA review consultation)
literature.outcomes: consumer choice (browser choice screen, default apps, NFC payments, account creation); enforcement gaps
literature.headline: Identifies four concrete consumer benefits after 18 months (iOS browser choice screen, default-app choice on iOS, contactless payments without Apple Pay, Google account without Gmail) while listing ongoing suspected non-compliance.
literature.summary_plain: Europe's consumer federation says the DMA has already given people more choice on their phones and Google accounts, but that enforcement against the big platforms must get tougher.
literature.quality: Qualitative stocktake without quantitative outcome data; author campaigns for strong DMA enforcement.
literature.citation: BEUC (The European Consumer Organisation) (2025), First bloom: increased consumer choice after eighteen months of the DMA, BEUC report BEUC-X-2025-101

literature.authors: Richard Feasey, Giorgio Monti, Alexandre de Streel (CERRE)
literature.title: Assessing and Improving the DMA's Impact (Issue Paper, DMA@2: Towards Stronger Governance and Evaluation?)
literature.method: review of available evidence (compliance reports, Commission annual reports, ad hoc studies) plus interviews with gatekeepers and business users; proposes evaluation framework
literature.outcomes: quality of evidence on DMA impact; evaluation framework and output indicators
literature.headline: Concludes that gatekeeper compliance reports, Commission annual reports and ad hoc studies to date 'do not provide a good basis for understanding the impact of the DMA' and urges mandatory gatekeeper data reporting.
literature.summary_plain: Brussels think tank finds there is still too little data to say what the DMA has achieved, and proposes the Commission force gatekeepers to collect and report the data needed.
literature.quality: Mainly an evaluation-design paper with interview input; no new quantitative estimates.
literature.interested_party: Project supported by CERRE members including Amazon, Apple, Google, DuckDuckGo, Mozilla, Qualcomm and regulators (ACM, Arcep, EETT)
literature.citation: Richard Feasey, Giorgio Monti, Alexandre de Streel (CERRE) (2026), Assessing and Improving the DMA's Impact (Issue Paper, DMA@2: Towards Stronger Governance and Evaluation?), CERRE Issue Paper, February 2026

literature.authors: Fiona Scott Morton, Alissa Cooper, Jacques Crémer, Amelia Fletcher, Paul Heidhues, Giorgio Monti, Rupprecht Podszun, Alexandre de Streel, Tracy Xu
literature.title: Comments on the First Review of the Digital Markets Act
literature.venue: Yale Tobin Center for Economic Policy, February 2026
literature.method: structured expert assessment of the state of DMA enforcement and compliance as of end-2025, with list of enforcement actions and their results
literature.outcomes: enforcement actions and outcomes; compliance challenges; recommendations
literature.headline: Reviews DMA enforcement actions and results to end-2025 and notes a broadly shared assessment that compliance reports alone are insufficient, recommending changes for the 2026 review.
literature.summary_plain: A group of economists and lawyers takes stock of what DMA enforcement has achieved by the end of 2025 and lists where it falls short.
literature.quality: Expert synthesis by a university policy centre; descriptive, no causal estimates; several authors also wrote other DMA pieces.
literature.interested_party: Authors include prominent advocates of digital platform regulation
literature.citation: Fiona Scott Morton, Alissa Cooper, Jacques Crémer, Amelia Fletcher, Paul Heidhues, Giorgio Monti, Rupprecht Podszun, Alexandre de Streel, Tracy Xu (2026), Comments on the First Review of the Digital Markets Act, Yale Tobin Center for Economic Policy, February 2026

literature.title: The Digital Markets Act: What Have We Learned after the First Years of Its Application?
literature.method: legal-qualitative review of Commission practice, case law and observable market effects
literature.outcomes: clarity of DMA concepts; practical impact; consumer digital rights
literature.headline: Asks whether the DMA has had measurable market effects and evaluates its practical impact in the light of Commission practice and case law (abstract does not report numbers).
literature.summary_plain: A Czech law professor reviews the first years of the DMA to see whether it has changed markets and improved consumers' digital rights.
literature.quality: Mostly legal analysis with qualitative impact discussion; low weight as empirical evidence.
literature.citation: Michal Petr (2026), The Digital Markets Act: What Have We Learned after the First Years of Its Application?, Białostockie Studia Prawnicze 31(1): 155-177

evidence_rating_previous: early and thin: Commission review is qualitative; three studies with causal designs on individual remedies (browsers, Amazon ranking, maps) and one small study on start-ups; headline benefits never measured
